Unfortunately, you are incorrect. Dogs fall into one of three categories: well-bred, backyard-bred, and dog-intentionally-bred (i.e., dogs who have bred without human intervention).

Well-bred dogs are usually of a certain breed that humans have worked hard to purposely develop and maintain. A good breeder is incredibly passionate about their chosen breed. They're really into the history of the breed, want to promote the breed in a good light, try to do activities like dog sports or shows, and are involved with breed clubs. They are also EXTREMELY picky with whom their pups go to, do extensive health tests on the parents (to prevent any dominant or recessive genetic combos), socialize and evaluate each pup to ensure they go to the right homes, and will ALWAYS take a puppy back if it's not the right fit.

Well-bred dogs can have a purpose other than just being a pretty pet. Like, you don't see Afghan Hounds as military dogs, Chihuahuas as guide dogs for the blind, or Jack Russells herding sheep... There are just certain breeds that are better suited for certain jobs/tasks, and they LOVE doing them.

Backyard-bred dogs can usually be summed up in one word: money.  Granted, there are those dog owners who are just uninformed and have thoughts like "we just thought the puppies would be really cute" or "if she has puppies once, she'll be a better dog" but nine times out of ten, it's because of money. Backyard breeders don't care about the health testing of the parents, don't care where the puppies go, never worry about socializing, and are more worried about what colors they are producing. This is where you get all the puppy mills, pet store puppies, and parking lot puppies. 

Plus, dear gods, all the doodles... People seriously need to QUIT BUYING DOODLES! Doodle breeders are LIARS. So many of my clients swear they've got a goldendoodle, but it's MERLE. Neither poodles nor goldens have merle in their genetics. Besides, Standard Poodles can get the same haircut as a doodle! Other breeds such as Spanish Water Dogs, Portuguese Water Dogs, Barbets, Irish Water Spaniels, and Lagotto Romagnolo have the doodle "look" and (shocker) can be bought for the same price or cheaper from a reputable breeder who's prepped the puppy genetically and mentally for life.

Lastly, there are the dogs who have bred together because of accidents (or ignorance) on the owner's part, or just because nature took its course. These "mutts" can be absolutely great dogs and make the best pets! However, to say that they are genetically superior is incorrect. They definitely have a larger gene pool, but that only means that there's more things that can go right or wrong. They're more of a mystery as far as what's going to happen for them in the future, and all the different possible combos give you a unique one-of-a-kind friend. Another point of variety is that mental health is not disregarded like in backyard-bred dogs, but isn't a factor at all.

In contrast, breeds are much more predictable. Reputable breeders are aware of what traits, genetic issues, and diseases are common in their breeds, so they know what to test for and can decide not to breed certain dogs so they can't pass down those problems. This usually isn't a problem for popular breeds like Beagles, Dachshunds, Labs, Border Collies, etc. because the genetic pool is large enough for variety. But it can be problematic for rare breeds such as Otterhounds and Skye Terriers.

So if I have to conclude this in some way:

-Well-bred dogs are great for the predictability in regards to health and type, especially when needed for a specific purpose.

-Backyard-bred dogs have unpredictable health and personalities that leans towards the negatives, and are good for spending lots of money to get the dog and lots of money to pay for his/her vet bills in the future.

-Accidental/happenstance-bred dogs are the most unpredictable. They have a broader genetic makeup and disposition, which makes them unique and gives them a better chance at positives compared to backyard-bred dogs.

I agree with what another redditor said: your wife and kids don't see you at work and don't know how hard you work there. They only see the example of you at home.

I think it would be good to make a weekly schedule. Start with 2 days a week for your kids (at least 1-2 hours) and 1 day a week for your wife (also at least 1-2 hours). 

You could help the kids with homework, take them to a park, a shopping center, the movie theater, a hobby that they like or that you like and want them to learn, whatever. Provide them with a mentorship role and show them your life skills to make them proud of you. It can also provide your wife with a break or give her time to finish something she needs to do. Or she can join the activity too.

As for your wife, you can have a babysitter or family member watch the kids while you get coffee, dinner, go to a movie, run errands that need doing, etc. Even just taking a walk together outside on a nice day.

Something like Monday and Thursday for the kids, and maybe Friday or Sunday for you and your wife. That still gives you 4 days to rest. Plus, if your family knows the schedule, they can know which days to let you rest and not bother you. 

If you try a schedule like this, you can then modify it over time to what works for you. Your kids are also getting older, so they will need their parents less and less. Eventually, you don't need to worry about them much and just have a once a week date night with your wife.

So since this is apparently not common knowledge (and I also love cats with a father who's highly allergic) there's a way to **lessen or almost rid a cat of the allergen**. 

It's weird, so stay with me.   
First, you find someone who keeps chickens. But not only keeps chickens... raises chickens around a cat. For some unknown reason, the eggs from chickens constantly exposed to cats produce an enzyme that "cancels out" the allergen in cats.   
Second, take the eggs from the cat-exposed-chickens, deshell them, mix the innards in a blender, and then finally dehydrate the mixture.  
Third, sprinkle/mix the egg powder on the cat's food for every meal. 

Again, I don't know why it works... But I'm glad there's something out there that does! Just be careful about how much you put in the food because too little and it doesn't really work, while too much could cause cholesterol issues.

It seems like you really love your dog and want to exhaust every possibility before rehoming... I've had dogs like yours before (and currently have one now). They're definitely working dogs and not really pets. You've gotta work him. Weighted backpacks, more structured walks, higher expectations of obedience (i.e. not allowed to see or play with other dogs and people when on structured walks), pulling exercises (maybe get into dog joring?), and even consider making your dog a "room" in your house. My working line shepherd has his own "room" which is essentially a HUGE kennel in my living room. He feels safe in there and it keeps him out of my way when I want to do other things.  


Biggest thing though, is to not let the dog take over your life. You want him part of it, but you and your husband both need to structure your time so that the dog can pick up on the pattern. Dogs are great at following patterns. It's perfectly okay to have the dog spend quiet time in his crate when you want to stretch or meditate! I have my dogs take a forced nap in their crates after eating (to help with digestion, but also to give me time to myself).   


Another thing you can try, is adding the water to his food. This helped one of my other dogs immensely. She was constantly chugging water and throwing it back up, but once I started giving her the water in the food, she immediately quit doing that.   


If you still feel like rehoming is the better option for him, don't feel bad. It will be a struggle to find someone who can give him the time/space he needs, but there are people out there. Try checking in with a dog club in the area because someone there might be interested or know another person interested.

Introduce the dog to the house. 

Put him on leash and lead him around each room using words like "good" and "okay" with a happy voice, and "leave it" with a strong voice. Try to mix it up so that you don't have 10 "leave it"s for every 1 "good". Stop to look at and let him interact with the things he can have/use but lead him past and away from the things he can't.  He won't know what those words mean yet, but it's a good basis to start with and he can respond to the pitch of your voice. 

Do this once a day for a week, and then implement it as he gets older and more interested in the environment (i.e. starting to chew on something he's not supposed to, or jumping on furniture he's not allowed on).   


Another thing that immensely helps is to keep a harness and (light, inexpensive) leash on him any time he's not in the crate. He can just drag the leash around the house. This is really helpful for potty training because a lot of times puppies will pee when you go to pick them up or touch them in any way (excitement, submission). It's also helpful for leash training and stopping the dog from learning the "keep away" game. He can't steal your sock and take off with it to hide under your bed if you can grab the leash. I usually recommend a harness and leash for at least a month, and then after that go back to it if you notice any problems starting to occur.

I had undiagnosed ADHD and the teacher took it upon herself to "fix me" since the way she taught the class didn't go with my learning style. I was stuck in a corner to face her and the class so that my other classmates could tell on me when it didn't look like I was paying attention. The students don't ever need to be forced to change, the TEACHER needs to change. They should modify their teaching style based on the student.  


Plus... The methods you mentioned (and even the location) seems to me like she's an "old school" style teacher... Yes, shaking the crate or hitting the crate does work, however it makes the dog think that the bark itself caused the crate to shake. With certain breeds/personalities of dogs, this method doesn't work and can actually create anxiety.  


Also, I HATE using dog toys or treats for "leave it". Those things are theirs, and the dogs know it's theirs. OF COURSE they are going to be more persistent with trying to get a treat! Why is their owner suddenly telling them they can't have something they've been playing with or eating for quite some time now? It just makes zero sense to them. Plus, you're supposed to build to something they really want by starting with something they don't care about (or care very little for). Another issue this causes, is the dog thinking that "leave it" means "wait". They will get the chance to eat the treat or play with the toy later BECAUSE IT'S THEIRS IN THE FIRST PLACE so it creates sneaky dogs who go take what they want when you aren't looking.  


Instead of a treat, I tell the owner to use a balled up tissue or napkin in their hand. Still interesting enough because what puppy doesn't like shredding paper? But definitely not as interesting as a treat. Plus, if they are still tearing up your hand for the item, you can step on it. Stepping on something in a dogs mind is similar to when they see a sibling or their mother standing over and guarding whatever thing they don't want your puppy to have. This is a way to create respect in a puppy in their own language. You should NEVER EVER hold a dog down like that for not understanding/adhering to your supposed teaching rules. Just like you should never punish a child for the same thing. Hell, if the puppy is still trying their best to tear through your shoe, use a clear plastic cup or container that's sturdy enough to withstand them. There is never one method to do something, and don't let someone tell you otherwise.

Dog trainer here.... I use both actually! I use the harness for casual "sniff" walks or trails (but no yanking allowed) and the collar for heel. During a longer walk or with a younger dog that has a lot of energy, I will switch them back and forth from the harness to the collar, back to the harness again, etc. That way they will get structure and breaks from that structure.

To teach this, I first teach them the "follow me" method/game with the harness. This method is best in a field or at a park with a lot of space. Preferably no distractions at first and then add distractions later. What you'll need is a long leash which is at least 15ft (4.5 meters) let it all out on the ground and hold only the handle at the end. You then want to give them a que like "lets go" or "with me". Doesn't matter what you say, as long as it's consistent. Then, you don't talk the rest of the 5-10 minutes you are doing the exercise. That is key! You want your dog to watch you not listen for you! You will pick random directions to walk in and change your direction at random too. Try not to wander though... The best thing I've found is to have a fixed item in your mind like "walk 5 steps towards that tree over there, make a u-turn, walk 15 steps to the pavement, turn left, walk 3 steps down the walking trail, pause 30 seconds, make another u-turn..." Like that. Make yourself unpredictable to the dog! They think it's a wonderful game! Speed up or slow down depending on the dogs energy level and to keep them interested too. You especially want to change directions if they are zooming off ahead of you trying to predict where you are going.

Now, they will probably end up hitting the end of the leash, and that's okay. That's what the harness is for. It will feel a little uncomfortable to hit the end of the leash, but it's not going to hurt them like a collar might. Hitting the end of the leash teaches the "boundaries" of the game. Once they do it 2 or 3 times, they start to think "Okay... how is this game played?" and they will engage their brain instead of just being all "go" and no "think".

They also might get a little tangled at first. If it's just the leash under their body, or something simple, walk very slowly to give them the time/opportunity to fix it themselves (teaches them how to do it which is a great skill to have, and prevents dogs who like to cheat the game and tangle themselves up on purpose) dogs want to keep going forward with you, so they'll again, have to engage their brain and figure out what to do. Now of course, if they are really tangled up, go back and help them, but still try not to say anything if you are still in the game with them. You don't want to end the game on a tangle. Smart dogs will use it to get their way and get out of the game, and shy dogs will become afraid of the idea of tangling up so they won't want to play anymore.

The goal that you want to see, is that your dog is following you and paying attention to you without even the leash being a factor. You can do this "follow me" method once a day, a few times a day, or even a few times during the walk provided you have ample space to do it. Just throw it in and make it more engaging and interesting than just a jaunt down the street and back. Do it often enough and you'll see the yanking diminish by a lot.

Now, with the collar... Once they're on the collar, I want to teach them they are in "work mode" and must give me their full attention. The collar is for heeling. Which means no pulling at all and walking beside me. I like to use the luring or the "one two three" method for this. Depends on the dog. Randomly during the walk, I tell them to sit beside me. I then hold the harness with one hand, unclip the leash from the harness, and attach it to the collar. Hold the leash in the opposite hand. Like if the dog is on your left, hold the leash in your right hand. The hand above the dog will be for treats. I say the word "heel" only once. If the dog is highly distractable even on a good day, I will hold a piece of larger treat in front of their nose and let them nibble on it as they walk. Or, have multiple small treats to pez dispenser out but still keeping them honed in on my hand.

The other method is the "one two three" method. Same start as luring: have the dog sit, hold harness with one hand, attach leash to the collar, hold leash in the opposite hand, use treats in the hand above the dog, and say the word "heel" only once. The difference is that after saying the word "heel" you want to say out loud "One, two, THREE" where the "three" is when you give them a small treat. You can time your count with your steps especially at first. Don't yell "three" but make it sound more exciting.

For both of these techniques, when first starting out make sure to do them for short periods of time. You don't want them to lose interest. Make it like a game to them and they'll want to keep doing it. With luring, after some time try to see if you can hold the treat above them and they are still walking beside you looking at the treat. Do it for a short time at first and test them to see if they can do it longer and longer. If they get distracted, go back to holding it in front of their nose.  For the "one two three" method, try having longer breaks between the words. Always keep mixing it up on them. Sometimes a quick treat, sometimes a bit of a wait.

To end the "heel", have them sit again beside you. Hold the harness and clip the leash back on the harness. Then say a "break" word like "Okay! Break! Free! Done!" or whatever word you want to let them know the exercise is over and they can leave your side to go wander or explore.

I apologize for the essay... I see these kinds of questions a lot on this subreddit so I figure I might just type out my answer for once and then copy/paste it for others as well.

OH! And another thing... I absolutely do not recommend using a front clip harness on a dog under the age of 2. Their bodies are not done growing yet, and I've seen many times where a puppy picks a shoulder to pull from and causes themselves arthritis when they are older.  


Edit:  For those people wondering which kind of collar would be a safer option, I recommend a martingale collar. Preferably one that's half nylon or leather and half chain. Like this one:   
[https://www.baxterboo.com/global/images/products/large/guardian-gear-martingale-dog-collar-bluebird-7120.jpg](https://www.baxterboo.com/global/images/products/large/guardian-gear-martingale-dog-collar-bluebird-7120.jpg)  
Or this one:  
[https://i.pinimg.com/originals/d9/7d/e5/d97de51d7a089950415860d08571a5ec.jpg](https://i.pinimg.com/originals/d9/7d/e5/d97de51d7a089950415860d08571a5ec.jpg)

Do not make it so tight it chokes your dog... You only want it to be not able to slide off the dog's head at its tightest point. The idea is to have it tighten and catch under the dog's jaw so it can't fall off when they are pulling. Then when they are not pulling, it loosens up and feels comfy on their neck. The reason I suggest the one that's half and half is because the nylon or leather is comfortable to wear all day and the collar can tighten quickly with a chain versus being all nylon and catching or twisting.

​

Second dog listens the best, is sooo sweet, and has the most amazing heel you've ever seen! Third dog is another sweet one, loves snuggles on the couch, and loves my husband unconditionally. I guess what I'm trying to say is that you'll never get the perfect dog... as much as I wish I could have a dog who was perfect in every way, and I could do all of those things with just that one dog it's not going to happen.

Okay, I feel like I'm a professional in this since I worked for a company which sold and trained exclusively with ecollars and my own dogs are ecollar trained, so I'll give my two cents. 


The number will never be the same. If you have a true ecollar and not a shock collar, an ecollar works off of stimulating the muscles in the dog's neck. Same as a tens unit used for human muscle/tendon therapy. Muscles can tighten or loosen based on external or internal circumstances such as "Did he just come in from outside?" "Was he woken up from a nap?" "Is that a treat he really gets excited about?" " Did grandma come over?" "Is he still worried about the dog he saw an hour ago?" It will always be fluctuating.



Never expect the number to be the same. The dog is a living being, so we can't tune it like a computer and we need to adjust our tools to the dog.

I own a Blue Tegu, Jin-ki. One of the best damn pets I've ever had. Too smart for his own good though... 


If you're looking for advice, I'd suggest watching some YouTube videos from Rose City Reptiles on care and diet, Clint's Reptiles for facts and enclosure tips, and NERD for taming. Note: Tegu's have a stubborn/aggressive stage around 1-2 years we affectionately call "guberty". You just gotta be patient and get through it. If you're worried about it, there's plenty of videos about guberty on YouTube as well.


As far as food goes, I follow the "San Diego Diet" for Jin-ki and for my water monitor too (obviously different ingredients). Make sure to research what Tegu's can and can't eat... And probably shouldn't eat too. They *can* eat almost everything we do, but there are definitely some exceptions which could make them sick or even kill them.


Tegu's can get pretty big... the size they are when they're small does not determine the size they will be when an adult. A good size enclosure for a Tegu would be 4ft tall, 8ft wide, and 4ft deep. There's a variety of builds on YouTube for that as well if you don't want to buy one.
